passage:
Thursday night. Everyone keeps asking how I am and I keep saying "I'm fine." Papa died six weeks ago. I go to work, I answer emails, I laugh at the right moments. Inside there is a grey nothing and sometimes a hot anger at nothing at all. I don't tell anyone because they have their own lives.
Today my friend Pranav sat with me at lunch and said, "Tell me about your father. What was his laugh like?"
I did not expect it. I said, "Loud. He laughed at his own jokes." Then I could not stop talking for half an hour, and the numbness cracked a bit.
— Deepak

qa.q: How long ago did Deepak's father die?
qa.a: Deepak's father died six weeks ago.

qa.q: Why does Deepak keep saying "I'm fine"?
qa.a: Deepak does not want to burden others, since they have their own lives. Behind it are numbness and anger that are hard to share.

qa.q: What did Pranav do that helped Deepak open up?
qa.a: Pranav asked about Deepak's father by name and about the laugh, instead of asking how Deepak was. That gave Deepak something specific and warm to talk about.

qa.q: How might Pranav have felt watching Deepak talk for half an hour?
qa.a: Pranav was probably relieved and glad the question helped, though Pranav may also have felt sad. Listening without hurrying was the gift.

grounding: A bereaved person insists they are fine for fear of burdening others, feeling numb or angry, and finds relief when a friend asks about the lost person.

passage:
Chat, Saturday night
Deepak: Hey, how are you doing? Haven't heard from you in a while.
Ankita: I'm fine. Busy at work.
Deepak: Okay. Is it alright if I ask about your Nani? I still think about the story of her pickles.
Ankita: ...
Ankita: She used to make them every June and hide the jar from us.
Deepak: What did the kitchen smell like?
Ankita: Mustard oil and raw mango. I keep opening the cupboard to smell it. Silly.
Deepak: Not silly at all. Tell me more whenever you want.
Ankita: I didn't want to bother anyone. I've been so angry and I don't even know at whom.

qa.q: What did Ankita's Nani make every June?
qa.a: Ankita's Nani made pickles every June.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when saying "I'm fine. Busy at work."?
qa.a: Ankita was hiding grief and anger, afraid of bothering people. The later message about not wanting to bother anyone shows the "fine" was a cover.

qa.q: What did Deepak do that made it easier for Ankita to talk?
qa.a: Deepak asked permission to ask about Nani, mentioned the pickles by name and asked a small, warm question about the kitchen. Deepak also said to tell more whenever Ankita wanted.

qa.q: How might Deepak have felt when Ankita finally wrote about the anger?
qa.a: Deepak was probably relieved and moved that Ankita trusted Deepak. Listening was the right thing, not fixing.

grounding: A bereaved person insists they are fine, and finds relief when someone asks about their Nani by name.

passage:
Three months after her father's death, Zainab went back to teaching at the small-town girls' school. To everyone who asked, she said, "I'm fine, Allah's will." She smiled at the staffroom, graded papers, ate lunch alone.
At night she lay awake, feeling nothing at all, and then suddenly furious at the ceiling fan, the neighbours' radio, everything.
One afternoon Uma, the old maths teacher, sat beside her under the neem tree. She didn't ask how Zainab was. She said, "Your Abbu, Rashid sahib, used to bring you to school on his cycle, na? I remember him ringing the bell twice at the gate."
Zainab's throat closed. "He always rang twice. So I'd know it was him."
"Tell me about him," Uma said.
And for the first time in three months, Zainab talked, and cried, and felt lighter.

qa.q: How many times did Rashid sahib ring the bell at the gate?
qa.a: He rang the bell twice at the gate.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling at night in those months?
qa.a: Zainab felt numb and then suddenly furious, hiding her grief behind "I'm fine" during the day.

qa.q: Why did Uma's approach work?
qa.a: Uma didn't ask how Zainab was; she named Rashid sahib and shared a memory of him, which gave Zainab permission to talk about her father.

qa.q: How did Uma likely feel as Zainab began to talk?
qa.a: Uma likely felt tender and glad, having sensed Zainab's hidden grief and found a gentle way in.

grounding: A bereaved young woman insists she is fine while numb and angry, and finds relief when a colleague asks about her father by name.

passage:
Everyone in the Malmö office agreed Oskar had come back strong after his grandmother's funeral. He answered emails fast, joined every meeting, and when asked, said, "I'm fine, thanks, really." He didn't want to be the sad one in the room.
But at lunch he ate at his desk, and once Mina saw him staring at his screen for ten minutes without typing.
On Friday she brought two coffees to his desk. "Oskar, your grandmother, Ingrid, she was the one who knitted, right? You showed us that ugly Christmas jumper."
He laughed, surprised, and then his eyes filled. "It was terrible. She made one every year. I have eleven."
"Eleven?"
"Eleven." He took a breath. "Honestly, I'm not fine. I'm angry that I didn't visit more."
Mina pulled up a chair. "Tell me about the jumpers."

qa.q: How many jumpers does Oskar have?
qa.a: Oskar has eleven.

qa.q: Why did Oskar keep saying he was fine?
qa.a: Oskar didn't want to be the sad one in the room and feared burdening others, while inside he was angry and grieving.

qa.q: What worked about Mina's approach?
qa.a: She brought coffee, named his grandmother Ingrid and a real memory, which let Oskar laugh, cry and finally admit what he felt.

qa.q: How did Mina likely see Oskar before Friday?
qa.a: Mina likely felt concerned, noticing he ate alone and stared at his screen, and suspected he wasn't as fine as he said.

grounding: A bereaved person insists he is fine, afraid of being a burden, and finds relief when a colleague asks about his grandmother by name.

passage: Two months after his brother's death, Pranav was back at the bank branch, first in every morning, last to leave. "I'm fine, really," he told anyone who asked, already turning back to his screen. At the team lunch he laughed in the right places and ate nothing. When the printer jammed, he slammed the tray so hard the whole row looked up, then muttered sorry. Pooja, at the next desk, noticed the photo he had turned face down by his keyboard. That evening, as they locked the cabinets, she asked, "Can I ask about Rohan? What was he like?" Pranav went very still. For a second she feared she had made it worse. Then he laughed, a real laugh. "He was terrible at cricket and never admitted it." He talked for twenty minutes. At the door he said, "Everyone avoids his name. I didn't know how much I needed someone to say it."

qa.q: What was Rohan terrible at?
qa.a: He was terrible at cricket.

qa.q: What does Pranav slamming the printer tray suggest?
qa.a: It suggests anger and pain held under "I'm fine", spilling out over something small.

qa.q: What could colleagues learn from Pooja's question?
qa.a: Asking about the person by name, like "What was Rohan like?", can open a door that "Are you okay?" does not, as long as the listener then lets them talk.

qa.q: What was it like for Pooja when Pranav went very still?
qa.a: Pooja feared she had made things worse, then felt relieved when he laughed and began to talk about Rohan.

grounding: Shows a bereaved man insisting he is fine while numb and angry underneath, and finding relief when a colleague asks about his brother by name.
